title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 6: Integrated psychosocial care plan for comorbid depression in breast cancer patients in low-resource settings

description.narrative:
A partnership led by the Pakistan Institute of Living and Learning, and the University of Sheffield aims to develop, implement, and evaluate a culturally adapted prevention and integrated psychosocial care plan for depressed breast cancer survivors that can be implemented across low-resource settings.
Breast cancer is one of the main causes of death in women across the world every year. Pakistan has the highest rate of breast cancer in women in South Asia. The unavailability of and costly self-paid breast cancer treatment adds to increasing significant distress among women, with women who do survive having higher levels of depression and anxiety. This impacts their treatment outcomes and increases chances of the cancer returning. Beginning in July 2024, the five-year project aims to improve the well-being of breast cancer survivors as well as promote awareness to assist with increasing chances of early detection. This award is built on earlier work: Moving on After Breast Cancer Plus (Moving on ABC Plus) in Pakistan, and intends to assess different methods of offering support through mental health care plans or a combination of treatments in survivors of breast cancer with depression in Pakistan. Research activities include the development and application of a suitable mental health care plan for women survivors of breast cancer in Pakistan.

The project has six objectives: 1. Develop and apply a suitable mental health care plan for women survivors of breast cancer in Pakistan (Workstream One). 2. Work with policy makers, patients, families, and other professionals to understand their views on how to make the mental health care plan available for all survivors (Workstream Two). 3. To understand the cost of breast cancer and depression in Pakistan and assess the cost-effectiveness of the proposed intervention (Workstream Three). 4. Develop a social media campaign to increase public awareness to help reduce the rate of breast cancer and bolster the identification of early symptoms (Workstream Four). 5. Train researchers and healthcare professionals in breast cancer research and ways of providing mental health support (Workstream Five). 6. Set up a system to collect information about people with breast cancer in Sindh Province, Pakistan (Workstream Six).

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 6: Smoking cessation for people with severe mental illness in South Asia (SCIMITAR-SA)

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMICs) research partnership, between The University of York and the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, India.
People with severe mental illness constitute one of the most vulnerable populations, with a life expectancy that is reduced by approximately 20 years. Much of this reduced life expectancy is driven by the development of multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs) in these populations. The greatest contributor to this inequality is the use of tobacco, and addressing this problem can result in the greatest health gains for people with severe mental illness. Beginning in July 2024, the four year programme will adapt and refine a treatment for tobacco use by people with severe mental illness in Bangladesh, India and Pakistan. The award will use valid and reliable tests to assess the success of the intervention before assessing the economic benefits of the treatment and identifying strategies which are most useful in delivering the treatment in mental health facilities.

The project has six objectives: 1. Develop and apply a suitable mental health care plan for women survivors of breast cancer in Pakistan (Workstream One). 2. Work with policy makers, patients, families, and other professionals to understand their views on how to make the mental health care plan available for all survivors (Workstream Two). 3. To understand the cost of breast cancer and depression in Pakistan and assess the cost-effectiveness of the proposed intervention (Workstream Three). 4. Develop a social media campaign to increase public awareness to help reduce the rate of breast cancer and bolster the identification of early symptoms (Workstream Four). 5. Train researchers and healthcare professionals in breast cancer research and ways of providing mental health support (Workstream Five). 6. Set up a system to collect information about people with breast cancer in Sindh Province, Pakistan (Workstream Six).

title.narrative: Proposal and Partnership Development Awards (PPDA) for NIHR Research and Innovation for Global Health Transformation (RIGHT) call 6 Stage 2 applicants

description.narrative: The purpose of Proposal and Partnership Development Awards (PPDA) funding is to improve the quality and likelihood of success of the projects funded through the NIHR Research and Innovation for Global Health Transformation (RIGHT) programme. Applicants that are successful at RIGHT Stage 1 and invited to submit a Stage 2 application are eligible for a PPDA, subject to satisfactory submission of a PPDA application. Not all Stage 2 applicants awarded a PPDA go on to secure RIGHT programme funding, therefore the details of PPDA recipients are not published. For RIGHT Call 6, PPDA were extended to 12 applicant organisations to support partnership development and the preparation of a RIGHT Stage 2 application.

Proposal and Partnership Development Awards (PPDA) provide funding of up to £10,000 for organisations applying to NIHR Research and Innovation for Global Health Transformation (RIGHT) programme funding to: 1. Support applicants to work collaboratively with all study partners to develop the stage 2 application 2. Enhance partnerships across the proposed research collaboration 3. Initiate preparation of study governance documentation (i.e. due diligence and finance assurance policies) PPDA funds must be spent between the notification of RIGHT stage 1 outcome and the submission of the RIGHT stage 2 application.

title.narrative: NIHR Research on Interventions for Global Health Transformation: Call 7

description.narrative: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)'s seventh Research on Interventions for Global Health Transformation (RIGHT) call. RIGHT funds cutting-edge interdisciplinary applied health research in key areas in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where a strategic and targeted investment can result in a transformative impact. RIGHT Call 7 supports equitable partnerships between researchers to generate new research knowledge and evidence on supporting research to develop and evaluate interventions for the early detection and management of metabolic risk factors for cardiovascular disease and stroke in ODA-eligible countries. UK and LMIC-based universities and research institutes were invited to submit applications. Research must be focused on improving the health and welfare of people in LMICs.

The aims of NIHR RIGHT Call 7 are to: 1. Deliver applied health research for the direct and primary benefit to the health and wealth of people living in ODA-eligible countries, with a focus on research to develop and evaluate interventions for the early detection and management of metabolic risk factors for cardiovascular disease and stroke. 2. Strengthen capacity for research and knowledge exchange through equitable partnerships between researchers and institutions involved in the research. 3. Promote interdisciplinary approaches to working (including, but not limited to: clinical medicine, health economics, statistics, qualitative and social sciences), to ensure that research objectives can be delivered. 4. Generate new research knowledge and evidence on interventions to improve health outcomes of people in LMICs.

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: Cardiovascular disease risk reduction in sub–Saharan Africa (CARisSA)

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership between the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and the Wellcome Trust Kenya Research Programme that aims to develop and evaluate a community-centred intervention for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction is proposed. This partnership, involving experts from the UK, Kenya, and The Gambia, focuses on addressing high CVD risks in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), especially in regions where CVD management is challenging due to limited resources and complex health system barriers.
CVD rates are high in SSA, with younger populations at risk due to untreated hypertension, high blood pressure and other risk factors. The research will take place in Kilifi County, Kenya, and Kiang West, The Gambia. These regions are selected due to their high CVD burden and existing research infrastructure support that facilitates effective data collection and carrying out the intervention implementation.
Commencing in March 2025, this award aims to address significant gaps in CVD risk management by implementing cost-effective, affordable, evidence-based solutions that are sustainable within the local health systems. The long-term goal is to improve CVD outcomes and make it easier to expand and use the approach in other areas with similar facilitated scalability and adoption across similar high-burden regions in SSA.
The award involves the designing and testing of a tailored intervention that includes several components, such as task-sharing with community health workers, using digital health tools, providing combination therapy, and forming peer support groups to manage overall CVD risk in high-burden SSA areas.

The award has five objectives:
1. Co-design a community-centered intervention for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction in sub-Saharan Africa.
2. Evaluate the feasibility of implementing the co-designed intervention in real-world community and primary care settings.
3. Conduct a cluster randomised trial to assess the effectiveness of the intervention on CVD risk factors and health outcomes.
4. Evaluate the economic viability and sustainability of the community-centred intervention for cardiovascular disease risk reduction.
5. Conduct a process evaluation to understand the factors influencing the success and scalability of the intervention.

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: Community pharmacies managing hypertension in Bangladesh and Pakistan (COPE-BP)

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership that aims to develop and evaluate a community pharmacy-based intervention to improve hypertension management among low-income urban residents in Bangladesh and Pakistan. By delivering hypertension care through community pharmacies, the team seeks to enhance access to care and reduce the risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs).
CVDs are the leading cause of death globally, and hypertension is the most significant modifiable risk factor for CVDs. In Bangladesh and Pakistan, a high percentage of individuals with hypertension remain undiagnosed, untreated, or have uncontrolled blood pressure, particularly among low-income urban residents who face significant barriers to accessing healthcare. Community pharmacies are widely accessible and frequently used by these populations but are not fully integrated into formal healthcare systems.
The long-term aim of the award is to reduce premature deaths and disabilities caused by hypertension and associated CVDs in Bangladesh and Pakistan. This intervention will enable community pharmacists to provide hypertension care, including blood pressure monitoring, medication adherence support, health education, and referrals to primary care physicians.
Commencing in March 2025, the award will map existing community pharmacies and engage with key stakeholders to understand the current practices and identify barriers and facilitators regarding the implementation of the intervention. The intervention will be tested via a feasibility study before undertaking a randomised control trial to assess the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the intervention in reducing systolic blood pressure.

The award has nine objectives: 1. Develop a context-specific intervention aimed at managing hypertension among low-income urban residents in Bangladesh and Pakistan through community pharmacies. 2. Explore the feasibility of delivering the intervention and refine methods and procedures for a large-scale trial. 3. Assess the effectiveness of the intervention in reducing systolic blood pressure among low-income urban residents aged 30 years and older with hypertension in Bangladesh and Pakistan. 4. Conduct a comprehensive process evaluation to understand the implementation process of the intervention and how the health system and urban context in each site influence its effectiveness and sustainability. 5. Develop a cost-effectiveness model for hypertension care and assess the long-term cost-effectiveness of the intervention, including the costs of scaling up and the value of investing in strategies to improve uptake. 6. Enhance capacity in applied research, leadership, and community-based hypertension management among researchers, pharmacists, and healthcare professionals in Bangladesh and Pakistan. 7. Establish Community Advisory Panels in each country to engage patients, families, and community members in the research process. 8. Work with key stakeholders to translate our project findings into policy and practice and enact plans to sustain research and its impact. 9. Disseminate the intervention findings through academic publications, policy briefs, workshops, print and social media, and community events.

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: SMARThealth Caribbean, a community-led digitally aided support system for cardiovascular disease prevention

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by The University of the West Indies which aims to develop a community-led digital support system for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in four Caribbean countries: Commonwealth of Dominica, Guyana, Jamaica and St Vincent and the Grenadines.
Due to commence in March 2025, the five-year project intends to work with research partners in India (the George Insitute for Global Health), the UK (Imperial College London and the University of Glasgow) and Canada (McMaster University) to reduce the risk of developing future diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and stroke. This has the potential to benefit women, their families/households, and communities and to strengthen regional health systems. This will be done via the delivery of the SMARThealth platform intervention for screening and managing cardiovascular disease risk factors in mothers who develop gestational diabetes (diabetes during pregnancy) or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (high blood pressure during pregnancy), and their families.

The project has four objectives: 1. To improve women’s cardiometabolic health in the first twelve months after gestational diabetes (diabetes during pregnancy) or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (high blood pressure during pregnancy). 2. To diagnose and reduce risk for diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and stroke in other adult household members. 3. To implement a community-based screening and prevention program leading to health systems strengthening for women and families after the six-week postnatal care period. 4. To build community awareness and develop clinical and research capacity around improving cardiometabolic health in the Caribbean.

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: Integrated, co-developed intervention for detection and management of cardiometabolic risk factors in older Indians (CARDIO-INDIA)

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership led by University of Leicester (UoL) and the Centre for Chronic Disease Control (CCDC) in India which aims to co-create, implement, and evaluate a community and health system-based intervention to improve the early detection, treatment, and management of metabolic risk factors for cardiovascular diseases among older people in India.
Heart disease and stroke cause the greatest number of deaths in India and are not always identified early enough. Older people are more at risk of these two conditions because they might not get enough physical activity, be overweight, or have high blood pressure or high cholesterol or diabetes. As such, they often face challenges in getting continued care and complying with treatment advice. The project team will work with older people, their caregivers and frontline health workers to design a contextually relevant innovative care package.
Commencing in July 2025, the award will deliver four interlinked work packages which will be guided by the community engagement and involvement activities. The intervention package will consist of a decision support system to aid doctors in providing guideline recommended care, an assisted telemedicine platform to seek specialist consultation where necessary, and a patient-facing mobile application to promote self-management.

The award has four objectives:
1. To conduct formative research to understand key challenges in the detection, treatment, and management of metabolic risk factors for cardiovascular diseases and co-create an intervention, engaging all relevant stakeholders (Work Package 1).
2. To implement the intervention and evaluate its effectiveness and cost-effectiveness in improving patient-related clinical outcomes in comparison to current care pathways (Work Package 2).
3. To understand the acceptability, barriers, facilitators to implementing the intervention for different stakeholders and at different health system levels (Work Package 3).
4. If the intervention is found to be effective, a toolkit will be developed to facilitate it's adoption across India and other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) (Work Package 4).

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: A Low-Cost, Scalable Treatment Strategy for Improving Hypertension Control in Low- and Middle-Income Settings

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership that aims to improve hypertension control in Nigeria and Sri Lanka.
Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a major global challenge, especially in regions such as Africa and Asia. The conventional treatment approach involves starting with one medication, subsequently increasing the dose, or adding another medication, but this is considered an ineffective and inefficient approach.
Commencing in March 2025, the proposed research aims to evaluate a new treatment strategy for managing hypertension, focusing on its effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness compared to usual care. This includes assessing hypertension control rates, budget impact, and implementation feasibility in primary care settings. In turn, this works to improve healthcare providers' skills and confidence, increase access to quality care among vulnerable populations, and reduce health inequities. Additionally, the award outputs seek to influence policy, potentially integrating the strategy into national health policies and ensuring sustainable hypertension control practices within primary care settings in Nigeria and Sri Lanka.

The award has four objectives:
1. Formative research: understand the context and refine and adapt the new treatment strategy. 2. Evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the new treatment strategy. 3. Evaluate the implementation of the new treatment strategy. 4. Evaluate the budget impact and cost-effectiveness of the new treatment strategy.

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: Co-creation of a national technology-enabled program for weight management in Thailand

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership which aims to improve weight management in Thailand. Heart disease is the number one cause of death in Thailand and obesity is one of the main causes of heart disease.
Technology has the potential to improve the quality of weight management services at a low cost. However, research is needed to ensure that these features would be equally accessible and effective for various disadvantaged groups in Thailand. This award aims to understand whether weight management programs that use technology can be an economical way for Thailand’s government to help people to lose weight and lower their risk of heart disease. Specifically, this research will work to reduce the risk of heart disease for 250,000 people in Thailand each year, with the potential for other countries facing similar challenges to also benefit.
Commencing in March 2025, this award will assess the current situation in Thailand to understand what issues are important for the weight management program to be effective before working with healthcare providers and overweight people to develop two weight management programs. These will involve technology at two different price points, making sure that they are appealing for the elderly, poor and those living in rural or remote areas. Both interventions will be tested via a large study involving 4,500 overweight people across 60 health centres in Thailand, comparing those who use the two programs with people who are only given some advice, before the cost-effectiveness of the programme and whether it offers Thai taxpayers value for money will be assessed.

The award has four objectives: 1. Undertake context (behavioural, technological, and organisational) analysis to inform intervention development. 2. Co-create technology-enabled interventions for two price points being considered by the Thai policy makers, and assess their acceptability to diverse socio-demographic groups. 3. Evaluate the effectiveness of intervention using a cluster randomised trial. 4. Conduct economic evaluation and develop service standards for the interventions.

title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: Community-based Research for Assessment, Detection and management of hypertension after pregnancy for LifetimE Benefit (CRADLE-B)

description.narrative:
A UK and low-and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership between King’s College London and University of Zambia bringing together experts in maternal medicine, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, nephrology, cardiology, midwifery, nursing, community engagement, public health, and nutrition, across Sierra Leone, South Africa and Zambia to support women with high blood pressure early after delivery.
Women who have high blood pressure during pregnancy are at higher risk of heart disease, kidney disease or stroke as they get older. Across the world, more women die from these diseases than from any other cause. Over three quarters of these deaths take place in sub-Saharan Africa. Our early research shows that the risks of developing high blood pressure after childbirth may be much higher in LMICs like Sierra Leone, Zambia and South Africa. Women have limited knowledge about the risks of ongoing raised blood pressure after pregnancy, and damage it can cause. They also struggle to access and trust care that is available.
Commencing in March 2025, the award aims to provide accessible, trusted, acceptable and affordable quality care to lower blood pressure and prevent long-term harm which will work to improve women’s current and future health, including later pregnancies.
The award will work together with women, families, communities, healthcare providers and policy makers in three countries to understand day-to-day barriers and facilitators for accessing and providing quality postnatal care before using findings to design a new monitoring pathway of women with high blood pressure. Point-of-care tests will be used to check for kidney and heart damage, which will bolster understanding of how to best collect information, and the extent to which this disease is affecting target communities (teenage girls, women who have lost their babies and those with disabilities) to plan future care.

The award has four objectives:
1. To work together with women, families, communities, healthcare providers and policy makers in Sierra Leone, South Africa and Zambia to understand day-to-day barriers and facilitators to access and provision of quality postnatal care, and to establish community partnerships.
2. To undertake a study of women with raised blood pressure in a previous or current pregnancy to understand what proportion of women develop longer-term or ‘chronic’ raised blood pressure and related damage to their body organs, using bedside testing for heart and kidney function.
3. To work together to develop and evaluate a new ‘community champion-led’ intervention in order to: improve women’s knowledge about high blood pressure care and long-term health risks; improve access to local care, for example, testing blood pressure during the first year after birth; improve trust in care through tailored community champion support for monitoring, healthy-living and taking blood pressure medicines and improve blood pressure and risk of damage to other organs.
4. To support training and development of local future research leaders including in research methods, management and governance.

title.narrative: Proposal and Partnership Development Awards for NIHR Research on Interventions for Global Health Transformation: Call 7 Stage 2 applicants

description.narrative: The purpose of Proposal and Partnership Development Awards (PPDA) funding is to improve the quality and likelihood of success of the projects funded through the NIHR Research on Interventions for Global Health Transformation (RIGHT) programme. Applicants that are successful at RIGHT Stage 1 and invited to submit a Stage 2 application are eligible for a PPDA, subject to satisfactory submission of a PPDA application. Not all Stage 2 applicants awarded a PPDA go on to secure RIGHT programme funding, therefore the details of PPDA recipients are not published. For RIGHT Call 7, PPDA were extended to 13 applicant organisations to support partnership development and the preparation of a RIGHT Stage 2 application.

Proposal and Partnership Development Awards (PPDA) provide funding of up to £10,000 for organisations applying to NIHR Research on Interventions for Global Health Transformation (RIGHT) programme funding to: 1. Support applicants to work collaboratively with all study partners to develop the stage 2 application 2. Enhance partnerships across the proposed research collaboration 3. Initiate preparation of study governance documentation (i.e. due diligence and finance assurance policies) PPDA funds must be spent between the notification of RIGHT stage 1 outcome and the submission of the RIGHT stage 2 application.

title.narrative: NIHR Global Health Research Development Awards: call 1

description.narrative: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)’s first Global Health Research (GHR) Development Awards call. The GHR Development Awards provides funding to increase the competitiveness of global health research applications led by researchers based in countries eligible for Official Development Assistance (ODA). Funding awards can be led by a principal investigator employed by a higher education institution or a research institute based in an ODA-eligible country. Through the programme, NIHR aims to support researchers to progress to larger awards and be better positioned to generate a high-quality internationally competitive proposal for research funding addressing needs identified in ODA-eligible countries. Funding is awarded for a 12 month period to support the underpinning work to develop high-quality research proposals.

1. Support the development of high-quality research proposals led by researchers in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) which directly target local needs and priorities.
2. Build global health research capacity and capability by supporting underpinning work to develop high-quality research proposals that will help award holders and their organisations secure further research funding from the NIHR and other funders.
3. Promote the development of equitable and sustainable research partnerships among collaborators, including communities and community organisations based in LMICs.

title.narrative: NIHR Development Awards Call 1: Tackling childhood obesity in Latin America and South Asia

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the Universidad Autónoma de Querétaro, Mexico that aims to tackle childhood obesity in Bangladesh, Mexico, and Pakistan.
In Bangladesh, Mexico, and Pakistan, overweight and obesity is common among children, posing serious risks to their health. Childhood obesity persists into adulthood and increases the likelihood of chronic diseases, including heart disease, diabetes, cancer, and mental health problems. The impact extends beyond individual health, straining healthcare resources and hindering economic growth.
Previous attempts to address childhood obesity have had limited success, underscoring the need for innovative and culturally sensitive approaches. These should address both individual and environmental factors and should be tailored to the specific contexts of these countries.
Commencing in January 2025, the twelve-month award involves the assembly of researchers, community representatives, and policymakers from the three countries to develop a research proposal aimed at tackling the epidemic of childhood obesity. Planned activities include a review of the latest research on the topic, training individuals in developing high-quality research proposals, consulting stakeholders, and defining important outcomes. Activities will be conducted through a combination of in-person and online engagements to maximise efficiency and inclusivity. The primary output of this award is the development of a research funding proposal to tackle the issue of childhood obesity.
The proposed research will fill critical knowledge gaps regarding prevention and management of childhood obesity. By involving children, parents, and teachers in the design process, the award will work to develop interventions that address various contributing factors, including diet, physical activity, sleep, and environmental influences.

The award has four objectives:
1. To strengthen the applicant team by identifying and inviting additional experts, policymakers, and representatives of relevant community organisations to participate in our research.
2. To build capacity to develop, submit and manage global health research awards and to engage communities in research.
3. To develop the future research programme by searching for the most important information gaps, refining research questions, identifying outcomes that are important to stakeholders, and writing the research funding application.
4. To establish equitable South-South and North-South partnership by agreeing shared values, equitable distribution of responsibilities, determining a transparent decision-making process, and achieving gender equity.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: A UK-South Asia Collaborative to address the impact of maternal micronutrient deficiencies on infant-neurodevelopment

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the Sitaram Bhartia Institute of Science and Research in India working in collaboration with partners based in Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka and key stakeholders across the health, policy and non-governmental organisation sector to understand how a lack of vitamins and minerals (micronutrients) in mothers and babies affects children's brain development and how it can be prevented and/or treated.
Vitamins and minerals are critical for maintaining health at all stages of life. Despite recent efforts to support children's growth, the problem of inadequate micronutrient intake among mothers and infants remains prevalent and under emphasised in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly within the most impoverished communities. Data indicates that deficiencies in certain micronutrients, such as Vitamin B-12, Vitamin D, or iron, can adversely affect a child's brain development. However, there is insufficient research on effective strategies to address these within LMICs. Addressing these gaps in knowledge is critical to preventing children in poorer communities from being left behind, perpetuating a cycle of inequality. The award explores key research questions aimed at addressing how the needed micronutrients can best be provided, whether the focus should be on single nutrients or multiple nutrients at once, and increasing the understanding of how restrictive diets during pregnancy affect micronutrient levels. Additional consideration will be given to whether to supplement mothers, babies, or both, determining the most appropriate doses and duration for identified supplements, and identifying and screening risk factors during pregnancy.
The award will involve a detailed review of existing research on the impact of micronutrient deficiencies on children's brain development, coupled with interviews, home environment assessments, and blood tests of a few mother-infant pairs from four countries. Current policies will form the basis of activities focused on the identification of potential enhancements, the arrangement of workshops to assess the efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability of proposed interventions which will be used to develop and refine a multicentric intervention plan along with identification and assessment of potential study sites. At the same time, the training and development of skills in South Asian partner countries will take place to build local capacity. The research team will work with government health administrations across South Asia to develop an evidence-based public health intervention plan, based on the tested interventions.

The award has four objectives:
1. To develop a multi-disciplinary partnership involving nutrition, maternal and child health and public health expertise in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. 2. To develop an understanding of key maternal micronutrient deficiencies and their impact on infant neurodevelopment. 3. To evaluate the national health policy framework of identified South Asian countries and propose a mitigation plan for addressing maternal micronutrient deficiencies. 4. To identify key research areas and to understand the feasibility of such work in the field including potential study sites and the ethics/data governance frameworks.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: A community based intervention against harmful use of alcohol in rural based settings

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by Makerere University, Uganda in partnership with Ugandan institutions: Mbarara University and Kabale University as well as Southampton University in the UK. Research activity is focused on conducting a pilot study which aims to provide an evidence base for a larger research proposal.
The Ugandan sub-region and location of the research is plagued with high levels of alcohol abuse that has affected health and productivity, and is associated notably with increasing poverty and domestic violence. Commencing in January 2025, the focus of the 12-month award is on the development, piloting and evaluation of a community-based peer support intervention to reduce the problem of alcohol use in Uganda. The study involves a systematic review of literature on intervention studies against alcohol abuse in rural settings, a survey on alcohol consumption patterns and a qualitative study of perceptions towards alcohol consumption.

The award has three objectives:
1. To review existing evidence on community-based interventions for reducing harmful alcohol use in rural areas of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), their effectiveness in different contexts, and potential mechanisms. 2. To conduct a survey to establish the level of harmful use of alcohol and factors associated with the behaviour. 3. To explore reasons for harmful use of alcohol, and perceptions on effective and acceptable ways of reducing the alcohol abuse.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: Co Producing a research agenda on climate change and refugee health

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the American University of Beirut, Lebanon in partnership with Imperial College London, UK. Refugees in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region have insecure living conditions. This makes them a vulnerable population to the increasing impacts of climate change through extreme weather events such as heatwaves, droughts, floods and sandstorms. There is a demonstrated need for climate-related vulnerabilities to be considered for refugees and the development of partnerships with academic, policy, community and humanitarian actors are important to co-produce solutions and policies that will reduce the health impact of climate change on refugee populations.
Commencing in January 2025, this one-year award aims to generate a research agenda about climate change and refugee health via the development of a conceptual framework and defining and refining research questions based on existing knowledge and the needs of the community and relevant actors. This award will establish a stakeholder advisory group to understand their key priorities and needs through interactive workshops, and work to identify the needs and priorities of refugees through refugee community group workshops and regular meetings. The main output from this award is the development of a proposal, which is based on established equitable partnerships, for a research programme that addresses the needs and priorities of refugees, decision-makers and humanitarian partners on climate change and refugee health.

The award has four objectives:
1. To establish new partnerships between the American University of Beirut, Imperial College London, and other Middle East and North Africa (MENA) regional partners on climate change and health. 2. To develop a conceptual framework for climate change and refugee health, and to define and refine research questions on climate change and refugee health based on existing knowledge and the needs of the community and actors. 3. To train and strengthen the team in writing research proposals and identified capacity building needs. 4. To design and develop a future research programme on climate change and refugee health that can be submitted for a relevant funding call.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: Towards Reducing Unnecessary C-Section via System Transformation in Bangladesh (TRUST).

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award, led by the International Centre for Diarrheal Disease Research, Bangladesh (ICDDR,B) which aims to address the issue of unnecessary caesarean sections (C-sections) in Bangladesh.
In recent years, Bangladesh has seen an alarming rise in C-sections in contrast to normal vaginal delivery. While C-sections can be lifesaving in certain circumstances, unnecessary C-sections carry significant risks and costs, making it a priority for the government and stakeholders in Bangladesh to reduce these procedures where appropriate. Although some progress has been made in policies and guidelines, along with increasing midwives and improving public maternity services for normal delivery, many women still opt for private facilities where vaginal births are significantly less common.
Understanding of the factors driving high C-section rates in Bangladesh remains incomplete. While profit incentives play a role, the issue is more complex. Further work is needed to identify these drivers and potential actions. The ultimate goal of the project is to collaboratively design a research programme aimed at developing and testing novel solutions for reducing unnecessary C-sections.
Commencing in January 2025, the twelve-month award will involve the review and compilation of existing research, before holding workshops with key stakeholder groups, including urban and rural women, midwives, nurses, obstetricians, women's health organisations, and policymakers. The award team will facilitate dialogues with diverse stakeholders in order to develop a shared understanding of the current situation and potential strategies for improvement. Individuals interested in joining a multi-stakeholder research team to develop a detailed follow-on research plan will be identified. Additionally, the award focuses on strengthening the research capacity and confidence of Bangladeshi researchers to lead large-scale research programmes.

The award has five objectives:
1. Summarise existing research on recent C-section patterns and drivers in Bangladesh, and interventions to reduce unnecessary C-sections. 2. Integrate stakeholder perspectives with research evidence to develop a shared understanding of the scale, drivers, and possible actions for unnecessary C-sections. 3. Build a consortium of individuals equipped to design and implement a new applied research programme. 4. Design a follow-on research programme to develop, pilot, and evaluate novel approaches to reducing unnecessary C-sections. 5. Strengthen health research capacity in Bangladesh.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: Intervention to strengthen low-and middle-income country primary care: proposal development for a cross-country comparison

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the Knowledge Translation Unit (KTU) of the University of Cape Town, South Africa, which aims to develop a research collaboration with key government, academic and community stakeholders and a proposal to conduct a comparative study evaluating the implementation of a primary care health system strengthening programme in South Africa, Brazil, Indonesia and Ethiopia.
The programme is called PACK, the Practical Approach to Care Kit. PACK is a system-strengthening programme that comprises a comprehensive clinical decision support tool for primary care and an implementation strategy that addresses health system barriers to its uptake. It has been introduced to all four countries to support primary care reforms and has shown some success in improving health outcomes and quality of care. However, there is limited evidence around how best to localise and implement the programme.
Due to commence in January 2025, the one-year award intends to evaluate how best to ensure that patient care is relevant to local diseases, health worker skills and available resources via the implementation of PACK within health systems in South Africa, Brazil, Indonesia and Ethiopia. While the award focuses on the development of a proposal centred on a cross-country comparative study of PACK implementation, activities also aim to foster research collaboration between KTU and key government, academic and community stakeholders. Increased collaboration between KTU and implementing partners works to bolster research skills, capacity and literacy, as well as efforts to ensure the most appropriate approach to measure successes and challenges of the programme are established.

The award has five objectives:
1. To convene a group focused on the cultivation of a research collaboration between implementing partners across four countries. 2. To identify and address the research collaboration’s capacity-strengthening needs. 3. To determine the research methodology required to conduct a cross-country comparison of the Practical Approach to Care Kit (PACK) implementation experiences. 4. To create a Community Engagement and Involvement methodology. 5. To generate a research proposal focused on the evaluation of cross-country PACK implementation experiences.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: Development of a research partnership for improving monitoring and treatment of neonatal infections in Bangladesh

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) led award led by the Child Health Research Foundation in Bangladesh which aims to establish a research partnership with the UK-based Centre for Antimicrobial Optimisation Network (CAMO-Net).
Neonatal deaths remain a major challenge to Bangladesh in its pursuit of achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030. Specifically, infections are a significant cause of neonatal deaths in Bangladesh, and the rise of antimicrobial-resistant infections continues to exacerbate this issue and threaten progress made. Commencing in January 2025 this partnership, known as the Bangladesh Initiative for Advancing Research on Neonatal Infections (BARN), aims to build clinical research capacity in Bangladesh to better monitor and manage neonatal infections. The BARN initiative will lay the foundation for the transfer of knowledge and skills related to cutting-edge biomonitoring and surveillance technologies from the Global North to the Global South, enabling their critical evaluation and use in LMIC settings. This will be done through the co-development of two pilot studies aimed at examining the use of continuing monitoring systems for non-invasive tracking of antibiotics and biomarkers in neonates to optimise antimicrobial usage, as well as to use molecular epidemiological methods to track and reduce healthcare-associated infections in neonates.

The award has five objectives:
1. To strengthen the ongoing partnership between the Child Health Research Foundation in Bangladesh and UK-based Centre for Antimicrobial Optimisation Network (CAMO-Net) through stakeholder engagement meetings. 2. To examine the use of continuous monitoring systems for non-invasive tracking of antibiotics and biomarkers in neonates to optimise antimicrobial usage. 3. To use molecular epidemiological methods to track and reduce healthcare-associated infections in neonates. 4. To conduct retrospective analysis of clinical and epidemiological data on neonatal infections available from four hospitals in Bangladesh. 5. To develop training workshops for early career researchers in Bangladesh, focusing on research methods, ethics, and project management.

title.narrative: NIHR Development Awards Call 1: Improving Outcomes for Patients with Fragility Fractures in the Philippines

description.narrative:
A low- and-middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the University of the Philippines Manila, Philippines in partnership with the University of Oxford, United Kingdom which aims to convene a community engagement group to explore and understand patient, carer, and healthcare provider experiences and priorities, map existing care pathways, and develop strategies to enhance recovery from fragility fractures.
Commencing in January 2025, this twelve-month award will undertake patient and carer interviews and hospital surveys to identify the facilities currently available for treating these patients in the Philippines. This work will inform a subsequent research proposal to improve patient outcomes, reduce healthcare costs, and influence national healthcare policy in the Philippines and other LMICs in Southeast Asia.
The number of people with fragility fractures is increasing in many LMICs. Asia is particularly affected by rapidly aging populations; a study in nine countries predicts a two-fold increase in the number of hip fractures alone, from just over a million in 2018 to more than two and a half million by 2050. Data from the Orthogeriatric and Fracture Liaison Service registry of the Philippine General Hospital show significant healthcare costs, with an estimated economic burden of PhP 1 billion per year (approximately USD 17 million). This may underrate the real situation, as the majority of hip fractures are still underreported due to economic and logistical reasons, and osteoporosis and fragility fracture treatment is not a priority of the Philippine healthcare system at present. No cost-effective treatment pathway of care for patients with fragility fractures is in place in the Philippines. Unlike hip fractures, most patients with a shoulder, wrist, or ankle fracture are not admitted to hospital but are treated as outpatients via the hospital fracture clinic; these patients’ disabilities compromise independence, quality of life, and productivity as well.

This award has three objectives:
1. To expand the existing Philippines Community Engagement and Involvement Group to include patients with shoulder, wrist, and ankle fractures and conduct in-depth interviews with patients aged 50 and above, and carers or family members. By exploring their experiences, challenges, and priorities during their recovery this will help identify key points in the care pathway where targeted interventions can improve outcomes. 2. To map capabilities in managing fragility fractures, particularly those involving the shoulder, wrist, and ankle through a comprehensive survey assessing service availability and service-specific readiness using the World Health Organisation Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) tool. 3. To create bespoke country-specific data to influence and change policy at a national and regional level to improve care for all patients with fragility fractures.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: A political economy and comparative analysis of the politics and governance of mobility in African cities.

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH), Uganda in partnership with the University of Rwanda and Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Malawi, University of Antwerp, Belgium and Canterbury Christ Church University, UK. Together this partnership aims to understand the political and governance dynamics of cities in order to inform mobility planning and contextually adapted strategies in Uganda, Rwanda and Malawi.
In the context of rapid urbanisation, African countries are grappling with how to manage emerging issues such as unplanned transport systems, accessibility challenges, traffic congestion and vehicle accidents. Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 11 focuses on making cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable with its achievement largely influenced by governance, politics and interests that shape how policy decisions are made and implemented. However, such broad health objectives, coupled with complex governance arrangements have received inadequate attention in the area of mobility and road safety within the African region.
Commencing in January 2025, the twelve-month award will draw on diverse methodologies, theoretical frameworks and empirical analyses to generate evidence which will inform a broader research proposal. Capacity enhancement efforts will be cross-cutting and pursued at individual, organisational and partnership levels. Core activities include knowledge generation via analysis of policies and a scoping review on the political factors and dynamics shaping mobility in African cities, coupled with stakeholder and partnership engagement, evidence needs assessments and capacity development. This award will provide opportunities for mutual learning across the partnership, research community and practitioners through a comparative approach, learning by doing, exchanges and embedded capacity-building activities. These insights will inform the development of broader research projects and wider partnerships which are the ultimate outcomes of this award’s activity.

The award has five objectives:
1. To map and characterise the mobility-related policies across relevant sectors and organisations in cities of Kampala (Uganda), Kigali (Rwanda), and Lilongwe (Malawi). 2. To conduct a scoping review on how contextual factors, actor relationships, and power dynamics shape the development and implementation of mobility-related policies in different urban contexts in the wider global context. 3. To engage decision-makers in the identification and understanding of context-specific evidence needs required for policy changes and implementation challenges related to advancing mobility. 4. To develop a partnership to foster capacity enhancement for interdisciplinary social science research on public health policy in select African university settings. 5. To widen partnerships and produce a proposal for a longer-term grant that develops a consortium approach to enhance expertise, knowledge and resources for political analyses, policy advice and influence at partner institutions to support mobility in African cities.

title.narrative: NIHR DA 1: A task for community health workers? Mental health care for people in disadvantaged communities

description.narrative:
A low- and-middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the University of Witwatersrand, South Africa, which aims to develop a research proposal for the co-design, implementation, and evaluation of a community health worker-based service for screening for serious mental illness and supporting people living with serious mental illness (PLSMI) in a peri-urban community in Gauteng province, South Africa, that is integrated with primary health care services.
The government-implemented community health worker (CHW) programme expects CHWs to identify and refer cases of common mental disorders, gender-based violence, and drug, alcohol and child abuse. However, little training is provided on the skills necessary to fulfil these roles nor on the skills needed to support PLSMI.
Due to commence in January 2025, the twelve-month award intends to develop a research proposal for future research on a community health worker-based model for PLSMI through community engagement and involvement. Award activity initially focuses on understanding community health workers’ (CHWs) perceptions of serious mental illness and how they perceive their role in relation to PLSMI. It will involve engagement with community representatives and key stakeholders including decision-makers in order to better understand the experiences of PLSMI, and the existing and prospective role of CHWs and service providers in supporting CHWs to provide care for PLSMI. The focus on community engagement within this award will work to establish a core group of community representatives to ensure the integration of community representation, provide capacity-strengthening activities for community members and facilitate the co-development of a research proposal.

The project has four objectives:
1. To understand community health workers’ perceptions of serious mental illness, the role of traditional and biomedical treatments, and how they currently perceive their role concerning people living with serious mental illness. 2. To explore with community members the potential role of community health workers can play in supporting people living with serious mental illnesses. 3. To engage with healthcare providers and decision-makers on whether and how the publicly funded primary care system might integrate and support community health workers working with people living with serious mental illness. 4. To map the evidence for components of a community health worker-based service for people living with serious mental illness via an evidence map.

title.narrative: NIHR Development Awards Call 1: Population-based heart failure feasibility study in Maputo, Mozambique

description.narrative:
A low-and-middle-income country (LMIC) award led by Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, Mozambique in partnership with the University of Glasgow, United Kingdom which aims to generate preliminary data on causes of heart failure in the Mozambican population, and demonstrate approaches to population-based studies within low-resourced African settings.
Pre-existing data suggests that heart failure in Africa varies from the rest of the world due to a prevalence within a younger age demographic. Additionally, there are different causes and risk factors for heart failure in the African context, which is limited to data collected from hospital patients and not inclusive of cases not managed in hospitals. To implement measures that can be effective in preventing and controlling heart failure, it is important to know exactly how it presents at the population level. As such, data generated via award activity will guide the design and implementation aimed at bridging the knowledge gap of data more representative of the country’s population.
Commencing in January 2025, the twelve-month award will engage with community leaders and local authorities before undertaking data collection across a rural and urban setting within Mozambique. As a result, the design and implementation process of this study will employ community engagement and involvement to ensure integration of community perspectives and experiences, and increased collaboration between teams at the University of Glasgow in the United Kingdom and Maputo Central Hospital in Mozambique will bolster capacity strengthening initiatives.

The award has eight objectives: 1. To demonstrate the feasibility of conducting a population-based study in a low resourced African setting and obtain preliminary data on the prevalence, aetiology and risk factors of heart failure in Mozambique. 2. To design and apply questionnaires to estimate the proportion of eligible people who are willing to participate, the proportion of participants who drop out and the standard deviation that will be used for the sample size calculation in the follow-up study on a representative urban and rural population sample of Mozambique. 3. To pilot-test study tools/questionnaires and measurement procedures for assessment of prevalence, risk factors and the diagnosis of heart failure. To describe the process for conducting population-based heart failure research in a low resourced African setting, including the challenges found and actions taken to overcome them. 4. To describe the process for conducting a population-based heart failure research in a low resourced African setting, including the challenges found and actions taken to overcome them during planning, patient recruitment and collection of epidemiological, clinical and biospecimen data. 5. To determine and compare the age and sex-specific prevalence of heart failure via questionnaire in a sample of both the urban and rural population of Mozambique. 6. To describe the antecedents (risk factors and aetiologies) and specific phenotypes of heart failure found in a sample of the population of Mozambique, according to residence in urban or rural area and socio-economic status. 7. To measure household expenditure, according to residence in urban or rural areas. 8. To evaluate the quality of life of participants, including heart failure patients, according to residence in urban or rural areas.

title.narrative: NIHR Development Awards Call 1: Co-developing a digitally integrated care pathway for maternity care

description.narrative:
A low- and middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the University of Colombo, Sri Lanka, with mentorship from the University of Birmingham, UK, which aims to reduce long-term complications and improve clinical outcomes and quality of life for pregnant women in Sri Lanka.
Due to commence in January 2025, the one-year award intends to manage hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, improve Sri Lanka’s maternal care information system for future research and assist health professionals in decision-making.
Sri Lanka is a low-middle-income country. Despite vast improvements in reducing the number of women dying during or soon after delivery in the country, quality of care and reducing complications and the development of pregnancy-related conditions is still an ongoing issue. Specifically, the award aims to form a diverse stakeholder group to provide comprehensive expertise throughout the project’s lifecycle and beyond, as well as co-creating a prototype of a digital Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) embedded within Sri Lanka’s Electronic Health Records (EHR) system with an initial focus on hypertensive disorders during pregnancy. Plans to generate a co-developed research proposal for funding to test and evaluate the EHR and CDSS system are also highlighted. These research activities provide an opportunity to improve in-country information systems in maternal care for future research, health system strengthening and eventually in establishing a learning health system.

This award has three objectives:
1. To establish an inclusive and representative stakeholder consultation group to provide comprehensive expertise throughout the project's lifecycle and beyond. 2. To co-develop a comprehensive maternity Electronic Health Record and clinical decision support system prototype for managing hypertensive disorders during antenatal care. 3. To co-develop an applied global health research proposal to improve antenatal care during pregnancy in Sri Lanka, and test and evaluate the prototype in antenatal hospital clinics.

title.narrative: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)’s first Global Research Professorship call

description.narrative: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)’s first Global Research Professorship call. The Global Research Professorships programme funds research leaders, with a track-record of applied health research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), to promote effective translation of research and to strengthen research leadership at the highest academic levels. Funding of up to £2m over up to 5 years is awarded to Professors working in close partnership with a research institution in an LMIC.

By the end of the award, NIHR Global Research Professors will be expected to:
1) Have demonstrated research leadership at a national and/or international level. 2) Have been developed and protected by their institutions, including being relieved of administrative tasks. 3) Enhance existing and establish new research collaborations in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). 4) Have supported training and capacity strengthening/mentorship within LMIC and UK (if applicable) institutions that enhances research capacity for future global health and care research.

title.narrative: NIHR GRP: Improving Adult Health in Sub-Saharan African Through Couples-Focused Interventions for HIV and Diabetes

description.narrative: The NIHR Global Research Professorship scheme is open to all professions and all Higher Education Institutions (HEI), based in England and the Devolved Administrations, to nominate health researchers and methodologists with an outstanding research record of clinical and applied health research and its effective translation for improved health. Global Health Research Professors are required to have existing strong collaborations or links with collaborators or partners in institutions in countries on the OECD DAC list and the award should plan to strengthen these/support training and capacity development/mentorship in these partners. The aim of this Global Research Professorship is to evaluate couple-focused interventions to reduce the burden of diseases in sub-Saharan Africa, in particular Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and diabetes. The majority of adults are in a partnership and to varying degrees live shared lives. Couples-focused interventions can be more effective than individual interventions in facilitating long-term behavioral change by one or both members of a couple.

To contribute to the design and evaluation of interventions for couples affected by Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), other Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and, diabetes in South Africa; support other research sites in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) to prepare for couples-focused research and evaluation; and develop capacity in the design of complex interventions, models and theory of behavioural change, and quantitative dyadic analyses. The research has three strands: 1) adapting an existing intervention to substantially enhance promotion of couples HIV testing and counselling among couples who have never tested together for HIV or mutually disclosed their status; 2) developing a couples-focused intervention for couples where one partner has diabetes; and, 3) establishing a research agenda in couples-focused health research in SSA

title.narrative: NIHR GRP: Translational Research to Reduce Mortality from Central Nervous System (CNS) Infections in Africa

description.narrative: The NIHR Global Research Professorship scheme is open to all professions and all Higher Education Institutions (HEI), based in England and the Devolved Administrations, to nominate health researchers and methodologists with an outstanding research record of clinical and applied health research and its effective translation for improved health. Global Research Professors are required to have existing strong collaborations or links with collaborators or partners in institutions in countries on the OECD DAC list and the award should plan to strengthen these/support training and capacity development/mentorship in these partners. Infections of the central nervous system (CNS) are major causes of mortality in low- and middle-income countries. This research aims to generate a detailed understanding of the aetiology of adult meningitis in this setting to inform diagnostic pathways and treatment strategies. The research group will evaluate affordable point-of-care diagnostic tests for meningitis, which are urgently needed to facilitate diagnosis, screening and prevention strategies, and trial novel effective treatments required to improve patient outcomes. The project is based in Botswana and the majority of the research will be conducted in this region.

To improve management of adult meningitis in African settings with high levels of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Key goals are (1) to collect information on all patients being tested for meningitis at an African hospital, and run very detailed testing to determine the causes; (2) to evaluate new tests for meningitis capable of testing for many different infections at once and diagnosing infection at the bedside; (3) to test a new treatment for cryptococcal meningitis (CM), the commonest cause of meningitis in this setting, based on a single very high dose of an existing drug called liposomal amphotericin; and (4) to perform a detailed examination of the patients’ immune responses and genetic make up to try to find out why some patients develop CM while some do not, and what factors are associated with death from CM.

title.narrative: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)’s second Global Research Professorship call

description.narrative: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR)’s second Global Research Professorship call. The Global Research Professorships programme funds research leaders, with a track-record of applied health research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), to promote effective translation of research and to strengthen research leadership at the highest academic levels. Funding of up to £2m over up to 5 years is awarded to Professors working in close partnership with a research institution in an LMIC.

By the end of the award, NIHR Global Research Professors will be expected to:

title.narrative: NIHR GRP: Preventing Invasive Salmonella Disease in Africa

description.narrative: The NIHR Global Research Professorship scheme is open to all professions and all Higher Education Institutions (HEI), based in England and the Devolved Administrations, to nominate health researchers and methodologists with an outstanding research record of clinical and applied health research and its effective translation for improved health. Global Research Professors are required to have existing strong collaborations or links with collaborators or partners in institutions in countries on the OECD DAC list and the award should plan to strengthen these/support training and capacity development/mentorship in these partners. Typhoid fever and Invasive Non-Typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) disease are two invasive blood-stream infections caused by bacteria called Salmonella responsible for serious illness and death particularly in young children in sub-Saharan Africa. This research aims to drive translational impact in the prevention of invasive Salmonella disease in Africa, with the major focus on accelerating and advancing the national and regional introduction of vaccination for Typhoid and for iNTS disease. The project is based in Malawi and the majority of the research will be conducted in this region.

To accelerate the vaccine prevention of Typhoid fever and Invasive Non-Typhoidal Salmonella disease. The research has 3 workstreams: 1.) Epidemiology: how much typhoid and iNTS disease are happening, and how do they spread in urban and rural communities? 2.) Protection: How do people’s bodies make protective immune responses against Salmonella infection, and how can we design better vaccines? 3.) Vaccines: How well do the vaccines actually work in healthy and immunosuppressed children? In addition Professor Gordon will support these workstreams with activities to discuss and explain Salmonella disease and research among the communities she works with, use research findings to engage with stakeholders and accelerated introduction of vaccines, and train the next generation of doctors and scientists in Malawi to be the researchers of the future.

title.narrative: NIHR GRP: Developing a melioidosis vaccine targeted for people with type 2 diabetes in Low- and Middle-income countries

description.narrative: The NIHR Global Research Professorship scheme is open to all professions and all Higher Education Institutions (HEI), based in England and the Devolved Administrations, to nominate health researchers and methodologists with an outstanding research record of clinical and applied health research and its effective translation for improved health. Global Research Professors are required to have existing strong collaborations or links with collaborators or partners in institutions in countries on the OECD DAC list and the award should plan to strengthen these/support training and capacity development/mentorship in these partners.Melioidosis is a grossly under-recognised tropical disease, caused by bacterium in the soil. Most people with melioidosis are poor and live in rural regions, typically working in rice farming. Ubon in Northeast Thailand is a world hotspot for melioidosis. More than half of melioidosis patients have diabetes, which is rising rapidly in low- and middle-income countries. This research will conduct the world’s first clinical trial of a new vaccine to prevent melioidosis, targeted for people with diabetes in Thailand and other tropical regions. The laboratory research carried out will identify which biomarkers to use to monitor how the vaccine works in Thailand, and study why people with diabetes are at a greater risk of infections compared to other people.

The aims of the research are: 1. To evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of a vaccine for melioidosis in people with diabetes in Oxford, UK, and compare immunogenicity with healthy non-diabetic subjects. 2. Characterisation of the impact of diabetes and ageing on infection and vaccination. 3. To define the key biomarkers (immune correlates of protection) for future monitoring of efficacy of the vaccine for melioidosis using an existing melioidosis patient cohort study. 4. To undertake a community consultation activity to explore perceptions, understanding and key sensitivities amongst people living with diabetes in Ubon Ratchathani, Thailand towards participation in future efficacy trials of a melioidosis vaccine.

title.narrative: NIHR GRP: Stopping mothers dying From Sepsis in Africa

description.narrative: The NIHR Global Research Professorship scheme is open to all professions and all Higher Education Institutions (HEI), based in England and the Devolved Administrations, to nominate health researchers and methodologists with an outstanding research record of clinical and applied health research and its effective translation for improved health. Global Research Professors are required to have existing strong collaborations or links with collaborators or partners in institutions in countries on the OECD DAC list and the award should plan to strengthen these/support training and capacity development/mentorship in these partners. Maternal sepsis is one of the most important causes of death and harm to mothers and their babies during or after pregnancy. It disproportionately impacts women and their families in low income countries. This research will improve our understanding of the epidemiology of maternal infection, optimise approaches to better prevent and diagnose maternal sepsis, and rigorously test at scale a facility level intervention aiming to improve maternal sepsis outcomes. The research will be focused in Malawi, and an important part of this programme will be working collaboratively with Malawian researchers to build maternal health research capacity.

This research aims to make major advances in the understanding of maternal infection in Malawi, and how to better prevent and manage these infections in order to reduce mortality and morbidity from maternal sepsis in Africa. The research programme workstreams are 1.) Understanding maternal infection in Malawi; 2.) Preventing infections; focussing on caesarean section and miscarriage surgery and 3.) Improving the management of maternal sepsis. Additionally, the research programme has two cross-cutting themes – 1) training and capacity building and 2) Communication with the public, practitioners, and policy makers.

title.narrative: NIHR GRP: Using participatory approaches to improve access to healthcare for disabled people in Uganda

description.narrative: The NIHR Global Research Professorship scheme is open to all professions and Higher Education Institutions in England and the Devolved Administrations, to nominate health researchers and methodologists with an outstanding clinical and applied health research record and its effective translation for improved health. Global Research Professors are required to have existing strong links with partners in institutions in countries on the OECD DAC list and the award should plan to support training and capacity development in these partners. There are one billion disabled people globally. Disabled people, on average, have higher healthcare needs than others, yet they face barriers in accessing it. As a result, they have worse health outcomes, including 2-3 times higher mortality rates across all ages. Policies and laws supporting the right to healthcare for disabled people are often not put into practice. Evidence is growing that interventions to improve healthcare led by communities are particularly effective. They are low-cost, scalable and address locally relevant concerns. One example is the Participatory Learning and Action (PLA) approach developed to prevent maternal and newborn deaths. In PLA, women’s community groups are established and meet monthly to: 1) identify problems, 2) identify solutions, 3) plan and implement solutions, and 4) evaluate their efforts. PLA significantly reduces maternal and newborn deaths, usually by at least 20%, and is endorsed by WHO. The aim of this study is to assess whether the PLA for Disability (PLA-D) approach can reduce mortality and improve health of disabled people in Uganda. Research will be undertaken by a consortium of UK and Uganda based partners. We will identify the problems facing disabled people in accessing healthcare in Uganda, through: 1) In-depth interviews with key informants (e.g. disabled people, health workers), 2) Analysis of existing numerical data, 3) Updating reviews on access to healthcare for disabled people. We will then collaborate with disabled people and health professionals to use this information to adapt the PLA approach for disabled people. We will decide who should facilitate the groups, where they should meet, and how to adapt PLA delivery and materials. Five PLA-D groups will be established, each including about 20 disabled people. We will assess whether they are feasible to run or need further adaptations. We will then undertake a trial to assess whether PLA-D is effective. We will identify 128 clusters (villages or city blocks) in Luuka district, and randomly assign them to be in the intervention or control group. In the control group, we will help to strengthen the health system, by undertaking an accessibility audit of health facilities and providing training on disability to healthcare workers. In the intervention group we will establish one PLA-D group per cluster, as well as the health system strengthening activities. We will interview all disabled people in the study about health and healthcare access at baseline and follow-up (1 year and 2 years), and record if any participants had died. The intervention and control groups will be compared to assess whether mortality rates were lower and health/healthcare access better in the intervention groups than among controls, and what the cost was for the outcomes achieved. Community engagement is at the heart of PLA as well as the Disability Movement with its ethos “Nothing about us, without us”. We will include disabled people as advisors at every stage, and as researchers wherever possible. We will hold community meetings and with disabled people’s organisations. We will engage with policy and programme implementers, both in Uganda and internationally, by producing short documents of key findings and holding meetings. We will reach academics through publishing articles in journals and presenting at meetings and conferences.

Objectives: To use an evidenced-based approach to co-create PLA-D. To assess the feasibility of PLA-D implementation. To undertake a cluster-based Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) to assess the effectiveness/cost-effectiveness of PLA-D in reducing mortality. To undertake a process evaluation of PLA-D to understand mechanisms for impact and scale-up. To strengthen capacity for informing disability policy and practice through the conduct of high-quality research.
